articles.title: Why Marco Rubio’s visit to Mumbai has ruffled feathers in India
articles.summary: US secretary of state is skipping New Delhi, and opposition leaders complain his arrangements are humiliating.
articles.body:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is to visit India in the coming week, but he will not set foot in the capital, New Delhi.

Instead, on Monday, Rubio will hold talks with Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in Mumbai, India’s financial hub, and then visit an oil refinery in Jamnagar in the western state of Gujarat, according to a statement from the US Department of State.

His itinerary sparked a political storm after the US ambassador to India said Washington expected Jaishankar to travel to meet Rubio, prompting opposition leaders to accuse the government of allowing India’s top diplomat to be “summoned” on home soil.

The spat comes as relations between the two countries are strained over trade, tariffs and India’s purchases of Russian oil.

So why is Rubio avoiding New Delhi, and why has it caused such upset? Here’s what you need to know:

He plans to discuss trade, energy and investment.

Rubio is arriving on Sunday from Samarkand, Uzbekistan, where he has been meeting with five Central Asian states at the C5+1 summit .

In India, he is due to meet senior officials to discuss the US-India strategic partnership and energy cooperation and hold talks with business leaders, the State Department said.

Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal appeared to confirm the agenda, stating on Friday that the Mumbai talks would cover energy, trade and investment, defence, and critical and emerging technologies.

In Jamnagar, Rubio is to visit the world’s largest single-site refinery, operated by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, and attend a reception hosted by the Ambani family, according to The Hindu newspaper.

Rubio was in the Indian capital in May for a meeting of foreign ministers of countries in the Quad, a group consisting of the US, India, Japan and Australia.

The State Department has framed his upcoming trip around energy and investment, and the second stop on Rubio’s India visit, Jamnagar, is one of the world’s most important energy hubs.

The visit also comes as fuel prices bite in the US before next month’s midterm elections.

Reliance, an energy, retail and telecommunications conglomerate, also sits at the centre of Washington’s wider oil diplomacy .

Business Standard, an Indian financial daily, said the Jamnagar stop was significant because Reliance is the biggest buyer of Venezuelan crude oil besides the US at a time when Washington has been urging India to buy more.

Since US forces seized Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January and took essential control of the country’s oil industry, the US government has marketed Venezuelan oil to buyers abroad.

Reliance is also investing in a new refinery in Texas, the first to be built in the US in 50 years, which Trump hailed as a $300bn deal when he announced it in March, Business Standard reported.

What did the US ambassador say, and why has it caused upset?

Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on Thursday, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said Rubio would meet Indian government officials in Mumbai, and Washington “expected” Jaishankar and others from New Delhi to travel there to see him.

Earlier in the week, however, Jaiswal had not confirmed the trip or explained why Rubio was skipping New Delhi, telling reporters the Indian government would announce it “at the appropriate time”, The Hindu newspaper reported.

Jairam Ramesh, a general secretary of the opposition Indian National Congress party, wrote on X that the ambassador’s statement was “quite extraordinary”.

Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition in parliament’s lower house, also took to X to comment, writing on Friday that Rubio had “summoned his employee to Mumbai”.

“A foreign government summoning India’s External Affairs Minister on Indian soil is a new low, even by the Modi Government’s standards,” he wrote on X, referring to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Mainly because of Trump’s tariffs and Russian oil.

In August last year after a round of trade talks broke down, the US hit most Indian goods with a 50 percent tariff. Under a framework the two sides agreed in February, that rate fell to 18 percent, however.

This month, Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the talks had “plateaued”, according to The Hindu.

On Thursday, Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said the “first tranche” of a deal was in its final stages but India would not sign until its exporters had an edge over rivals such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Indonesia, according to the Reuters news agency.

Last week, US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced that his department was suspending eight companies – including the Indian IT giants Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL – from a labour certification scheme that is a key step for employers seeking green cards for their foreign staff.

Sameer Lalwani, a senior fellow in the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, wrote this week that Indian public opinion of the US has hit a record low, citing US engagement with Pakistan and the US-Israel war on Iran, which he said had pushed India back towards Russian oil.

Despite that, he argued, defence and technology cooperation has quietly deepened, and bilateral trade grew by almost 12 percent in 2025 to nearly $240bn.

In his view, “perceptions of the political relationship have deteriorated faster than its strategic foundations.”

A sanctions law had threatened to make matters worse.

Last month, Trump signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which could impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian oil or gas.

India, one of the world’s biggest buyers of Russian oil, had warned Washington that new tariffs could hurt bilateral ties. Trump signed an executive order seeking to waive the sanctions on Friday as he tries to ease high oil prices before the November 3 US elections.

articles.title: Student grievances, cost-of-living crisis, political discontent: Why are protests turning violent in France
articles.summary: France’s student-led protests over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating school facilities have widened into a nationwide movement
articles.body: France’s student-led protests over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating school facilities have widened into a nationwide movement fuelled by economic anxiety, anger over police conduct and growing political discontent ahead of the 2027 presidential election. The demonstrations, which began in the Paris suburb of Créteil in mid-September, have drawn in trade unions, parents and activists associated with the Yellow Vest movement, with some protests escalating into clashes, arson and looting.On Saturday, looters targeted luxury boutiques, an Apple Store, supermarkets and other businesses across several French cities as demonstrations against the cost of living intensified. The unrest spread across Paris, Marseille, Lille and Nice, with reports of vandalism, fires and confrontations with police. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the weekend's clashes had resulted in more than 1,200 arrests and 150 injured police officers, while President Emmanuel Macron vowed to prosecute those involved in violence and looting.The protests have evolved from demands for better educational resources into a broader expression of frustration over inequality, purchasing power, public spending and a political establishment struggling to address competing demands. The approaching presidential election has added another dimension, with political parties seeking to influence the movement and position themselves ahead of the 2027 vote.Also read - Watch: Historic French town hall burnt, tear gas fired as 5,50,00 protest in FranceHow the protests beganThe unrest began on last month in September, when students at Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, an underprivileged suburb of Paris, protested against a shortage of substitute teachers, overcrowded classrooms and inadequate school facilities. Students and teachers raised concerns about deteriorating educational standards and classrooms that had become difficult to use following summer heatwaves.The movement spread through social media, with students blocking school entrances and piling rubbish bins outside campuses to prevent access. Demonstrations soon reached cities including Lille, Bordeaux, Marseille, Lyon, Nantes and Rennes. What began as a localised dispute over school conditions developed into a wider campaign against inequalities in education and the government's handling of public services.The grievances reflect a broader concern that students in under-resourced public schools face disadvantages compared with those attending better-funded institutions. In France, access to elite higher education and the career opportunities associated with it remains a central route to social mobility. Protesters argue that unequal school conditions undermine the country's stated commitment to equality.The mobilisation gained momentum as public-sector workers prepared to strike against government budget proposals. By late September, the student movement was intersecting with opposition to spending cuts and plans to rein in public finances, creating a wider platform for dissatisfaction with the government.From school blockades to street violenceThe first major escalation came as student demonstrations coincided with public-sector strikes in late September. The Union Syndicale Lycéenne called for national action, while students at hundreds of schools blocked entrances using bins and barriers. Although many demonstrations remained peaceful, confrontations were reported at several locations, with police deploying tear gas and protesters throwing objects and setting rubbish bins on fire.By September 30, the education ministry said around 400 schools had experienced protests or disruptions. More than 440 people were detained, most of them minors, according to officials. The unrest continued into October, with fires reported at schools and clashes spreading to additional cities.The response by law enforcement became a major source of anger. On October 5, a 15-year-old boy lost his hand after a police grenade exploded during a protest in Lens, northern France. The incident intensified criticism of the authorities' handling of demonstrations and sharpened concerns about the use of force against young protesters.The scale of mobilisation grew further on October 6, when high school students were joined by university students, teachers, parents and trade unionists. Estimates of participation ranged from 256,000, according to the government, to 450,000, according to unions. While many marches began peacefully, violence broke out in several cities, including Paris, Lyon and Rennes.The government subsequently promised to recruit 3,000 substitute teachers and review school hours. Student unions rejected the proposed measures as insufficient, and further strikes and demonstrations followed. By October 13, cars had been set ablaze and riot police had used water cannon and tear gas in Paris and Nantes.Why the cost-of-living crisis mattersThe student movement has expanded amid growing anxiety over household finances and purchasing power. France's cost-of-living pressures have added to dissatisfaction with the government, particularly as fuel prices have risen since the start of the US-Iran war earlier this year. The economic strain has helped bring the student protests closer to the concerns of workers and other groups already critical of government policy.The Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in 2018 and 2019 in opposition to fuel taxes and wider economic grievances, has again become part of the protest landscape. Its earlier demonstrations reflected resentment among people who felt that economic decisions made in Paris placed a disproportionate burden on households outside the country's wealthier circles.Trade unions have also opposed the government's proposed budget savings and public-sector pay restraint. France has been trying to rein in its public deficit while dealing with a mounting debt burden. The draft 2027 budget includes a proposed €54 billion savings drive, which has become a focal point for opposition among public-sector workers and others concerned about the future of public services.This has created a difficult balancing act for the government. Authorities are under pressure to control public spending, while students, teachers and unions are demanding more resources for schools, better working conditions and measures to protect purchasing power. The convergence of these demands has helped turn a school-focused movement into a broader protest against economic and political priorities.Inequality and anger over educationThe protests have also exposed longstanding concerns about inequality in France's education system. Students have complained about teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating facilities, arguing that poor conditions disproportionately affect disadvantaged communities.The movement's origins in Créteil, a working-class suburb outside Paris, have reinforced concerns about unequal access to educational opportunities. Students from underfunded public schools may find themselves at a disadvantage compared with peers who attend better-resourced institutions and have greater access to academic support.These concerns extend beyond school infrastructure. Protesters have raised questions about whether France's promise of equality is reflected in the opportunities available to young people from different social and economic backgrounds. The concentration of political power, elite education and economic opportunity in Paris has also contributed to resentment among communities that feel neglected.The protests have drawn support from parents who believe demonstrations are necessary to force the government to address educational inequality. Three students told the BBC: “France likes to speak of égalité, but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit”.The demonstrations have also revived memories of the May 1968 student movement, which grew into a major general strike after workers joined the protests. The latest mobilisation has similarly expanded beyond campuses, although its immediate demands and the circumstances surrounding it are different.How protests turned into urban riotsThe movement underwent a major transformation on October 17, when student groups, labour unions and Yellow Vest activists converged during nationwide demonstrations. The protests, which drew more than 550,000 participants according to figures cited in the supplied material, were accompanied by widespread violence and looting in several cities.In Paris, looters broke into shops near République Square, throwing skincare products and mobile phones into crowds. A nearby bar, La Barrique, was ablaze, while the monument at the square was covered in graffiti and paving stones were ripped up. Youths also broke into a supermarket and threw bottles and cans at police officers.In Marseille, protesters vandalised dozens of shops, including luxury brand Hermès and businesses selling jewellery, clothing, cosmetics, household appliances and bread. Firefighters responded to a blaze at a shoe shop. In Lille, an Apple Store was targeted, while shops, sportswear outlets and a motorcycle dealership were looted in Nice.Other reports described attacks on public buildings and state symbols, including a fire that severely damaged Limoges town hall and an attack on Marseille City Hall. A tourism office in Lyon was also reported to have been set ablaze. The incidents marked a shift from school blockades and marches to widespread attacks on businesses and public property.The violence has complicated the movement's demands for educational reform and economic relief. While many demonstrators have focused on school conditions, public spending and inequality, looting and arson have prompted a tougher response from authorities and given political leaders grounds to condemn the unrest.Political battle ahead of 2027 electionThe protests have unfolded as France prepares for its 2027 presidential election, with political parties seeking to position themselves around public anger. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has accused the radical-left La France Insoumise (LFI) party of exploiting the student movement for electoral gain.“Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage,” Lecornu said on Wednesday, accusing the party of encouraging protests while condemning violence.LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon has attracted support from demonstrators who back proposals including a wealth tax, improved education and lowering the voting age to 16. The party's position has placed it at the centre of the political debate over how the government should respond to the unrest and the demands behind it.The election has also intensified wider political competition. Marine Le Pen's National Rally and Mélenchon's LFI have drawn support from voters disillusioned with the political establishment, albeit from opposing ends of the political spectrum. The protests have created another challenge for the government as parties seek to translate economic anxiety and dissatisfaction with public services into electoral support.The political divisions reflect a wider crisis of confidence in the country's institutions. France's fragmented parliament and difficulties in building stable governing coalitions have complicated efforts to agree on spending priorities and economic reforms. The approaching election has increased pressure on political leaders to respond to public anger while avoiding commitments that could worsen the country's financial position.Government faces pressure to restore orderThe French government has condemned the violence while acknowledging the need to address the grievances behind the protests. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu faces pressure to tackle teacher shortages, poor school infrastructure and public service dissatisfaction as his government tries to rein in spending and manage the country's mounting debt.President Emmanuel Macron vowed action against those involved in vandalism and looting, saying: "those who carried out vandalism, attacked administrative offices or businesses, or carried out looting -- even in our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished".The government faces the twin challenge of restoring law and order while addressing demands for better education, relief from rising living costs and greater equality. While injuries to police personnel and damage to shops and public buildings have intensified calls for a crackdown, the injury to a teenage protester has fuelled criticism of the police response. With France set to hold presidential elections in 2027, the government's handling of the protests could influence the political debate in the months ahead.You use AI every day. articles.title: AI tool helps stranded protesters find their way home in the Indian capital
articles.summary: A lifeline that connects people detained and dropped off at distant locations with volunteers who ensure a safe return.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – A 19-year-old woman was detained by police during the youth-led antigovernment protests in the Indian capital over the weekend.

The young woman, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of further reprisals from the authorities, said she was detained on Sunday as thousands of people congregated in central New Delhi. They were demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls, which saw the removal of 133 million people from the voter lists.

After the woman’s detention, she and several other demonstrators were taken on a police bus to a location about 50km from the protest site. With no cash and her phone battery drained, the woman spent nearly an hour wandering along a dark road, trying to figure out what to do next.

A car pulled up and the driver asked if she needed any help.

“I was frightened and completely lost. When those volunteers finally helped me get back safely, it felt like a miracle. I had never imagined that someone I had never met would come forward to help me like that,” she told Al Jazeera.

For a young woman in New Delhi, notoriously referred to as the “rape capital of India”, being alone in the middle of the night and getting into a car with strangers is not an easy decision. The city records an average of three rapes a day.

But the young protester said she immediately recognised one of the volunteers in the car. She had seen his videos online, in which he had asked the detained protesters whether they needed help. Recognising a familiar face reassured her that the people offering the ride could be trusted.

The woman was rescued using an AI-assisted tool developed by 25-year-old Rajiv Choudhary, who is helping protesters get home safely after being detained and dropped off by the police far away.

Called the Detainee Gharwapsi Yojana, the initiative combines a digital dashboard with a network of volunteers who track information about police buses carrying detainees and arrange transport for those left stranded.

“Gharwapsi” in Hindi means “to return home”. It is also a play on a campaign by India’s right-wing Hindu groups which want to bring the country’s Muslims and Christians back into the Hindu fold, claiming that their ancestors converted to “foreign” religions from Hinduism. “Yojana” means a plan.

Since the beginning of this month, India has seen near daily protests over alleged electoral fraud by Kumar and his commission. Led by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a number of left-leaning student groups as well as the main opposition Congress party, the protests have seen tens of thousands of people hitting the streets in New Delhi and other cities.

In response, authorities in the Indian capital have imposed a sweeping crackdown, blocking roads, closing metro stations and detaining thousands as Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government faces the biggest challenge to its power after 12 years of rule.

Choudhary said his network’s primary focus was to help minors, elderly people and women, mainly first-time protesters.

The initiative operates through a private digital dashboard that uses AI-assisted data processing, live mapping and information shared by volunteers on the ground. Volunteers send details, including police bus numbers and locations, through WhatsApp, helping the team coordinate assistance and rides home.

Choudhary said he and his associate, journalist Meghnad, who goes by a single name, initially worked with a small group of volunteers to connect detainees with transport, legal assistance and medical support. The network has since expanded to more than 130 volunteers, who have offered their time and resources to assist detained demonstrators.

“For people caught up in these demonstrations, the ordeal doesn’t end with detention. They can be taken far from the protest site and left trying to find their way home from unfamiliar locations, often struggling to contact friends or arrange transport,” he said.

The idea grew out of Choudhary’s experience during an earlier protest called by the CJP at Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in New Delhi that has now been denotified by the authorities. Initially, he helped organise supplies and volunteers.

As demonstrations continued, he recognised that protesters needed more systemic support, particularly those who were detained by the police and left fending for themselves far from the city limits.

As renewed protests began on October 2 , Choudhary built a digital system around the same volunteer network using AI tools. It began with a simple spreadsheet.

“The whole aim behind the application was that I had to systemise things that are not systemised,” he said. “We just wanted to become a support system that could help our people in their fight for their demands.”

Choudhary recalled receiving a distress call from a woman who had been detained in central New Delhi and released on the outskirts of the city. Stranded alone near a railway station, with metro services shut and no clear way to get home, she was frightened and unsure which way to turn.

She reached out to Choudhary’s network for help and he arranged for a nearby female driver to take her home safely. “It is heartbreaking to see people left helpless in an unfamiliar city, frightened and unsure of how they will get home,” he said.

For now, the Detainee Gharwapsi Yojana operates only in New Delhi, but Choudhary plans to expand it to other cities.

“I am overwhelmed by the response from volunteers and drivers who have come forward to help without charging anything. They are offering their services for free because they want to support the protesters,” he said.

The 19-year-old woman who was helped by Choudhary’s team described the initiative as “a lifeline for protesters”. She said the team not only arranged her return, but also offered reassurance and emotional support.

“I cannot thank them enough. As long as we have people like them in our society, no authority can stop us from demanding our rights and protesting peacefully,” she said.

articles.title: Guatemalan former prosecutor shot dead at sports centre
articles.summary: Guatemalan police say they arrested two men in connection with the killing of Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa.
articles.body:
Lawyer Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa, known for his high-profile cases against powerful businessmen in Guatemala, has died after being shot by two men during a visit to a sports centre.

The attack on Saturday at the Campo Marte sports complex in Guatemala City resulted in the deaths of Foppa and another man, Gustavo Adolfo Aguilar Gamarro, according to the Public Prosecutor’s Office.

Shortly after, the Guatemalan police said they arrested two men and seized a carbine-style firearm and a motorcycle in connection with the case.

Foppa was a 43-year-old former prosecutor and anticorruption lawyer who denounced wrongdoing by some of Guatemala’s most powerful politicians, business leaders and companies, and in 2023 briefly joined the defence team of a prominent journalist.

President Bernardo Arevalo condemned the attack. “I strongly condemn the cowardly murder of former prosecutor Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa,” he wrote on his official X account. “Both the direct perpetrators and those who ordered the crime must face the full weight of the law.”

Arevalo said he has instructed his government to coordinate with the relevant authorities to solve the crime.

“Those who believe that terror can intimidate the people of Guatemala and the government I lead are mistaken. In honour of Foppa, in honour of our homeland, in honour of justice.”

Foppa headed the Criminal Investigations Directorate within the Public Prosecutor’s Office before he took charge of Guatemala’s tax authority (SAT) from 2016 to 2018, when he helped prosecute dozens of powerful Guatemalan business figures and recover unpaid taxes.

In 2025, Foppa alleged a connection between the Barrio 18 gang and the National Unity of Hope party, as well as links between criminal gangs and the judicial system. In 2023, he briefly joined the defence team of Guatemalan journalist Jose Ruben Zamora, who has become an international symbol of resistance to the criminalisation of journalism and the erosion of judicial independence in Central America.

Foppa had to leave the Zamora case after being accused by the Public Prosecutor’s Office of obstructing the proceedings and destroying or concealing information, a charge he denied but ultimately accepted as part of a plea agreement, saying he did not believe he would receive a fair trial.

articles.title: ‘Pandal will collapse’: Video captures announcement that may have triggered Kolkata stampede
articles.summary: KOLKATA: “The condition of the pandal is very bad. It will collapse.
articles.body: KOLKATA: “The condition of the pandal is very bad. It will collapse. Please leave.” A microphone announcement warning visitors that the Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal was at risk of collapsing may have triggered panic and contributed to a stampede that killed 19 people and injured 25 in north Kolkata on Saturday evening, police said on Sunday.A video of the announcement, which is being examined by Kolkata Police, captures the warning that the pandal could collapse. Police are trying to identify who made the announcement and establish what prompted it.Chief minister Suvendu Adhikari blamed the alleged callousness of the organisers and said the tragedy would be investigated. He also suggested that the announcement made by the puja committee over the microphone may have triggered the crush.A senior police officer said preliminary findings pointed to a combination of poor crowd management, confusing announcements and a sudden surge of visitors seeking shelter from a downpour during Saptami celebrations.“We have gathered sufficient evidence pointing to gross mismanagement by the puja organisers. There was no clear plan to manage the large number of visitors, and everything was handled verbally,” the officer said.Police have collected CCTV footage and recorded statements from locals and eyewitnesses. Investigators are also examining whether inadequate deployment of police personnel and private security guards worsened the situation.According to police, the gates and approach road to the pandal were narrow. As panic spread, visitors attempted to escape through the entrance, contributing to the crush. Announcements regarding entry, exit and crowd movement were also inadequate, leaving people confused amid the rush.Police said they would question survivors to cross-check eyewitness accounts and reconstruct the sequence of events. A forensic team visited the site on Saturday night to collect evidence, with another team expected to conduct further examinations.Meanwhile, Kolkata Police Commissioner Ajay Kumar Nand imposed prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita on roads adjoining the pandal until October 20.The state government has announced compensation of Rs 25 lakh and a Group D government job for the family of each deceased victim. It has also constituted a panel to review safety protocols at major Durga Puja pandals and recommend immediate corrective measures wherever shortcomings are found.Of the 25 injured, 14 were undergoing treatment at a private hospital on Sunday, with three in the intensive care unit. articles.title: Masked settlers attack European diplomats in the occupied West Bank
articles.summary: Masked settlers attacked a group of European diplomats during a visit to the occupied West Bank on Saturday, Belgium’s foreign minister said, on a second straight day of high-profile assaults on Palestinians and others during the sensitive olive harvest.
articles.body: JERUSALEM — Masked settlers attacked a group of European diplomats during a visit to the occupied West Bank on Saturday, Belgium’s foreign minister said, on a second straight day of high-profile assaults on Palestinians and others during the sensitive olive harvest. At least four people have been killed and more than 100 injured since the harvest began earlier this month, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry. Activists say Israeli authorities do little to stop attacks that involve weapons ranging from slingshots to guns. An attack Friday seriously injured a Washington Post photographer and others. In Saturday’s attack in the Christian village of Taybeh, settlers targeted Belgium’s consul general, French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives, Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said. “A French mayor was assaulted and a Belgian vehicle damaged. Our team is safe,” Prevot said. He linked the attack to what he called Israel’s “illegal settlement policy” and pledged to push for further European Union sanctions. “Impunity for violent settlers must end,” he added. Video shared by an activist at the scene, Amit Orfali, shows the French mayor, wearing a tricolor sash, leaning against a vehicle while sitting on the dusty ground. Other clips showed young masked men knocking insistently on a driver’s side window and asking for IDs, while other masked men carrying sticks advanced in the distance. Orfali said the masked men “threatened to kill us.” The attacks came less than two weeks before closely contested elections that could end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s time in office. His government, the most nationalist and far-right in Israel’s history, faces domestic criticism over security failures and international criticism over the treatment of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Some of the government’s senior officials are settlers themselves. Israel’s military in a statement confirmed Saturday’s attack on the diplomats and called it a “severe act of violence,” but said the visit had not been coordinated with it and no soldiers were at the scene. Israeli police said they had opened an investigation and vowed to work “until everyone who took part in these cases is brought to justice.” Foreign Minister Gideon Saar on X condemned the “severe acts of violence by Israeli rioters,” adding that his ministry was in contact with ambassadors from the countries concerned. But Netanyahu’s office later issued a statement warning against “premature conclusions” in the incident and noted concerns about “a coordinated campaign to smear Israel.” Netanyahu’s main rival in the elections, Gadi Eisenkot, said on X that “a handful of criminals is burning up the last shreds of legitimacy left to the state of Israel.” Eisenkot called it “Jewish terror” — the same term the photographer for The Washington Post, Heidi Levine, used when speaking to The Associated Press on Saturday from her hospital bed. “I’ve been covering this region for over 40 years, and I have never seen this country in such a state as it is today,” Levine said, adding that she was “shocked and insulted” that Netanyahu referred to the attack on her and others as an alleged one. Netanyahu in the past has attributed the violence to a small number of troublemakers. But cars have been burned, trees damaged and people hurt in communities across the Palestinian territory, with some people calling this the most dangerous season yet. The U.N. and much of the international community consider the settlements, many of them resembling developed suburbs, in the West Bank to be illegally occupied. Settlers have established hundreds of additional outposts without government authorization, while still enjoying protection from the Israeli military. Israel captured the West Bank, along with Gaza and east Jerusalem, in the 1967 Mideast war, territories the Palestinians want for a future state. The West Bank remains under Israeli military rule. The United States wants Israel to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers in the West Bank, U.S. Secretary ⁠of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday. “We’re very disturbed by those images and what we’re seeing,” Rubio said. “We’ve asked the Israelis and continue ⁠to ask them to crack ​down ⁠on that stuff.” One of the latest criticisms has come from China, whose foreign minister, Wang Yi, told Israeli President Isaac Herzog this week that Israel should “stop and revoke the act of forcibly establishing settlements in the West Bank,” a spokesperson said Friday.

articles.title: Rural communities exposed to heating oil costs, minister says
articles.summary: The government plans to regulate heating oil prices after increases.
articles.body:
Some people say they are finding it hard to heat their homes after increases in heating oil costs fuelled by the US-Israeli war with Iran.

Residents in the South West told the BBC they have held off buying fuel for the winter in the hope prices could come down and feared some people might go without.

It comes as the government announced new measures aimed at regulating the market and reviewing the minimum amounts some people have to buy.

Heating fuel costs have risen by up to 82% since the start of the conflict, according to the Minster for Energy Consumers Polly Billington.

Billington told the BBC: "We need to make sure the market is working as fairly as possible."

She said it was "striking" how rural communities with "so many people off grid" were "some of the most exposed" to the price increases.

Nicola Sharpe, from Dunsford, Devon, said this time last year she was paying about £340 for 500 litres, but the price was currently just over £600 for the same amount.

"I'm looking at ways to spread the cost when I have to bite the bullet and get it," she said.

Earlier in October, the government promised better regulation of the sector .

Ministers said they would tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things went wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, would also be reviewed.

Sharpe said she was not hopeful the government measures would help.

"I can't see how regulating it is going to bring costs down."

Pauline Trubody, from Porkellis, Cornwall, said she had already spent more on two deliveries of 500 litres this year compared to previous years.

The 76-year-old said: "I probably won't put it [the heating] on as much as I would have.

"There is going to be a lot of people who can't afford it and folk who are going to go cold."

Lee Fossey, from St Agnes, Cornwall, pays £30 a month into a savings scheme to spread the cost of heating oil throughout the year.

She said: "I have done everything I reasonably can to budget and prepare for winter, yet despite this, the dramatic increase in prices means I can no longer afford to fill my tank."

She said she faced the prospect of having no heating this winter or using the money for an alternative heating source.

Prices have soared since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran. In March, the government announced a support package worth £53m for low-income families who use heating oil.

articles.title: From village pub to Potato Queen: How Poppy O'Toole built a food empire
articles.summary: Poppy O'Toole says the foundations of her success were laid much closer to home in the Midlands.
articles.body:
Before she became known to millions online as the "Potato Queen", Poppy O'Toole was peeling potatoes in a village pub kitchen.

Now a chef, author and TV regular, O'Toole has built a huge following through social media, published six cookbooks and become one of Britain's best-known food personalities.

Known to viewers from programmes including Saturday Kitchen and This Morning, the Bromsgrove-born chef's journey began much closer to home.

She remembers cooking calamari after school at the age of 11, leaving her mother wondering why her daughter had decided to deep-fry squid instead of reaching for more conventional after-school snacks.

"I've just always loved food," she said.

Her first paid kitchen role came at a care home, where she prepared simple meals and delivered food and drinks to residents.

She explained how the experience showed her how much comfort food could bring, but she also cherished the conversations she had with residents, many of whom were living with dementia.

"I used to get told off so much there because I'd chat to every single person," she said.

She later took a job at The Queen's Head in Stoke Prior, initially working front of house before persuading staff to let her into the kitchen.

After impressing colleagues with a homemade pecan, caramel and chocolate tart, she was allowed to help with food preparation, including one task that would later prove fitting.

"One of my first jobs was peeling all the potatoes."

At the time, a career built around potatoes would have seemed unlikely.

O'Toole eventually secured an apprenticeship at Birmingham's Michelin-starred Purnell's after being encouraged to apply by her now husband, Tom.

She spent about three years there, before moving on to other kitchens in Birmingham and later, London.

The move south brought roles serving high-end banking clients and working at a private members' club in Mayfair.

Like many hospitality workers, O'Toole lost her job when lockdown restrictions forced venues to close. With the industry on hold, her husband suggested she start sharing cooking videos online.

"He'd been saying since we were about 18 that I should be doing social media," she said. "I thought everybody from work would watch it and it would be embarrassing."

After some early success, a series of potato recipes transformed her fortunes. A clip showing crispy cubed potatoes attracted huge attention and inspired what became her popular "25 Days of Christmas Potatoes" series.

Her popularity extends beyond potatoes, however. O'Toole said food should bring comfort and enjoyment rather than guilt, arguing that people are often encouraged to overthink what they eat.

"We're taking some of the enjoyment out of everything," she said.

As her following grew into the millions, so did her reputation as the "Potato Queen", a title she has embraced despite insisting potatoes deserve more respect.

"People always say 'the humble potato'," she said. "They're not humble. They're the best thing on the planet."

The success led to TV opportunities, including appearances on the likes of Saturday Kitchen and This Morning, as well as a stint judging BBC Three's Young MasterChef.

"It was amazing and horrible because you have to judge people," she joked of the role.

She revealed that many of the judges' remarks were first delivered to an empty studio before contestants enter, allowing producers to capture multiple camera angles.

Alongside her TV work, O'Toole continued writing cookbooks.

Her latest release focuses on batch cooking, an idea she developed while balancing work with pregnancy and new motherhood.

Recipes were tested repeatedly to ensure they could be frozen and reheated successfully, sometimes requiring four attempts before making the final manuscript.

A mushroom and truffle risotto repeatedly failed when frozen and reheated, ultimately forcing her to abandon the dish altogether.

O'Toole admitted she still found it strange to reflect on how far she has come.

Long-term, she still dreams of opening a business of her own, perhaps even a pub, although she says her husband is quick to point out the financial realities.

For now, however, her focus is on expanding her YouTube channel and creating content with the freedom to be herself.

"It was lovely working in TV," she said. "But on YouTube you get to do what you want to do."

articles.title: Huddersfield artist uses show to address violence against women
articles.summary: Prathiba Batley is taking her immersive performance 1,000 Papercuts to York University in October.
articles.body:
An artist using theatre to explore themes of surviving sexual violence and harassment has said performing is "cathartic and challenging at the same time".

Dr Prathiba Batley, founder of Eyakkam Dance Theatre in Huddersfield, uses dance, spoken word and music in her show 1,000 Papercuts to highlight her own experiences.

Through different forms, including Bharatanatyam - an Indian dance style - and playing the cajón drum, she said she could "democratise art forms" and address stereotypes.

"Most women, especially South Asian women, are expected to sit with their legs crossed. We don't make noise, we don't talk too much. Here I am, saying, 'I'm going to sit on this cajón, I'm going to make noise'."

"If that means I sing and dance and fight and speak, I will do all of that," Batley said.

"1,000 Papercuts is about getting people to understand what's happening on stage, so we can think about what to do next."

According to Batley, the show, which has received Arts Council England funding, reflected her own experience as a survivor of sexual abuse and workplace harassment.

She described it as "a difficult labour of love" to put together, but one that conveyed an important message.

"It is cathartic and challenging at the same time because you relive that trauma every single time you go into the studio space or into the theatre," she explained.

"The purpose behind Eyakkam is not just about physical movement, it is a social movement.

"It is something I use to move into the milieu of current issues, to address social justice, to talk about things that are pertinent to our life."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at BBC Action Line .

Batley said she worked with mental health professionals and a women's centre in Kirklees to develop the show.

"We want to be careful because there will be triggers, but you want to also have an impactful presentation," she said.

"That's how it came about with care in mind, but also with this crux of activating people."

The performance ends with a Q&A session which allows the audience to be connected to local services, including mental health charities.

1,000 Papercuts was co-produced by Lawrence Batley Theatre, and will be performed at York University on Saturday 28 October.

Touring the show, as well as developing the show into the Tamil language, would allow her to "reach a wider audience" and increase "audience participation", Batley added.

"Hopefully, we can create relationships between audiences and the services available in that location, and give them all these toolkits to take back with them.

"So, not just stop at performance, but continuing to activism, continuing to impact in daily life."

articles.title: Wedding content creator from Dorset says new industry is booming
articles.summary: A growing industry is helping newly weds post video content on social media 24 hours after their big day.
articles.body:
From the nerves before the ceremony to the tears of laughter during the best man's speech, Jade Burton is documenting every moment on her smartphone.

The 22-year-old, from Poole in Dorset, is one of a growing number of wedding content creators - a job that did not exist just a few years ago.

She films and edits social media-ready videos, giving newlyweds a record of their day just 24 hours after they say "I do".

For couples eager to share their big day on Instagram and TikTok, it's a service bridging the gap between the wedding itself and the professional photos that arrive weeks later.

As guests mingle in the autumn sunshine and staff put the finishing touches to the reception room, Burton hovers with her phone.

She started her wedding content creator business, Wed In Focus, in July.

"With the way technology's evolved and the rise of social media, naturally the way we document memories has changed a lot over time," she said.

Unlike a traditional videographer who might take a few months to produce a polished wedding film, Burton edits short-form, vertical videos called highlight reels that can be shared the next day.

"It'll kind of tell the wedding story, right from getting ready, through to first looks and ceremony, walking down the aisle - all the key moments."

Industry experts say the number of content creators has grown rapidly since first appearing in the UK wedding market in 2022.

Wedding website, Hitched, reported a rise in searches for wedding content creators in 2025.

Nikita Thorne, the UK Wedding Association's digital wedding expert and head of strategy at Oxfordshire-based Guides for Brides, said it was down to a combination of social media's growing influence on weddings and the relatively low cost of launching a content creation business.

"We've seen more content creators coming in the last couple of years where more people have been able to start a business," she said.

Thorne said the average price for a wedding content creator can range between £200 and £1,000 and usually covers the day of filming and the time spent editing.

The promise of receiving the memories within one day is proving attractive to some couples.

Between greeting guests and posing for photographs, bride Emily Errington knew there would be moments she would miss.

She hired Burton alongside a photographer and videographer to capture her wedding in Symondsbury, near Bridport in Dorset.

"I want to be looking at stuff straight away," she said.

"Right now it's all a bit of a whirlwind. I don't really know what's going on."

The couple banned guests from taking their own photos during the ceremony, knowing they would have the social media content to post themselves the following day.

"I don't want people to share videos or pictures without me having a say-so or seeing what it is that they're putting out there," she said.

"It's more for us to let the world know than anyone else."

But experts caution the growing popularity of the role has also attracted newcomers to the industry.

Thorne said the "relatively low barriers to entry" meant some people could try and do the job, despite having little experience of working at weddings.

Urging couples to check experience and credentials, she said: "A lot of people, while they might have relevant experience, such as working in social media, they're not experienced in wedding delivery."

Back at the wedding, Burton is weaving between tables and scanning the room for reactions she might otherwise miss.

She is keen to challenge the idea that the role simply involves pressing record on a smartphone.

"I think there's more to it than meets the eye. You have to have a good eye for composition, lighting, storytelling. Anticipating moments is really important.

"There's one take of the ceremony - you can't miss it."

articles.title: Heavenly bamboo was introduced to America in the early 1800s as an ornamental shrub; its red berries can poison birds as the shrub invades forests
articles.summary: Introduced to America as an ornamental plant in the early 1800s, heavenly bamboo has become a concern in parts of the country because of its ability to
articles.body: Introduced to America as an ornamental plant in the early 1800s, heavenly bamboo has become a concern in parts of the country because of its ability to spread into natural areas and its toxic berries. Despite its name, Nandina domestica is not a true bamboo. Native to Asia, this evergreen shrub is grown for its foliage, seasonal flowers and clusters of red berries. However, it can establish itself beyond gardens, spread through vegetative growth and seeds dispersed by birds, and compete with native vegetation. Its berries contain high levels of cyanide and can poison birds and other animals. The shrub’s spread and toxicity have prompted the Missouri Department of Conservation to advise against planting it and recommend removing established plants.What is heavenly bamboo and why is it considered an invasive plant?Heavenly bamboo, also known as nandina or sacred bamboo, is an evergreen shrub in the barberry family. Native to Asia, it is cultivated for its upright stems, compound leaves and ornamental appearance. The plant typically grows about 3 to 7 feet tall, although its size can vary depending on growing conditions.Its leaves may change colour through the seasons, while its small pinkish-white flowers generally appear in early summer. These are followed by clusters of red berries that can remain on the plant from autumn into spring. The berries contribute to its ornamental appeal but are also a source of concern because of their toxicity. The shrub was introduced to the United States as an ornamental plant in the early 19th century. It has since become established in parts of the country, particularly in the Southeast, where it can grow outside cultivated settings and spread into forests and other natural habitats.How heavenly bamboo spreads into natural areasHeavenly bamboo can spread through vegetative growth and seed dispersal. Its roots can produce new shoots, while birds that eat the berries can carry seeds away from the parent plant. However, the relative importance of these methods is not settled across the available sources. The US Forest Service’s review of the species reports that seed reproduction may be more common than vegetative reproduction, although the prevalence of each method is not well documented. The Missouri Department of Conservation, meanwhile, highlights the plant’s ability to regrow from its roots. Both pathways can contribute to its spread, and established plants can be difficult to eradicate.Once established outside cultivation, heavenly bamboo can form dense growth that competes with native plants. Its persistent foliage can shade native wildflowers, while dense thickets can limit food sources for wildlife by displacing native vegetation. The shrub’s spread has been documented in Tennessee forests. The Missouri Department of Conservation reports that heavenly bamboo has covered about 10,000 acres of national forest lands in Tennessee alone. Separately, a US Forest Service species review estimates that the plant covered 9,237 acres in Tennessee forests, based on Forest Inventory and Analysis data dated March 15, 2008. The figures refer to different descriptions of the land covered and should not be treated as directly comparable estimates.Why the red berries can be dangerous to birdsThe Missouri Department of Conservation states that heavenly bamboo’s berries contain high levels of cyanide and can poison wild birds and other animals, including pets. The department documents deaths among cedar waxwings that gorge on the berries, particularly when other types of berries are scarce. The risk does not mean every bird that eats the fruit will be poisoned: the department notes that most birds consume only a few berries at a time and are largely unharmed.Birds also contribute to the shrub’s spread. After eating the fruit, they can deposit undigested seeds far from the parent plant, allowing heavenly bamboo to establish in new locations. This creates a potential double problem: heavy berry consumption can be dangerous to some birds, while seed dispersal can help the non-native shrub spread into natural habitats.Should heavenly bamboo be planted in gardens?The Missouri Department of Conservation advises against planting heavenly bamboo and recommends removing it where it is already growing. The department also notes that no human poisonings have been reported in its account. However, it identifies the plant as toxic and warns of risks to pets and livestock. Removing established plants can require attention to the roots, as regrowth may occur if even a small piece remains in the soil. According to the department, cutting down or burning the above-ground growth can result in resprouting. Control methods may include pulling seedlings, cutting, prescribed burning and herbicide treatments, depending on the situation.Gardeners looking for alternatives can consider native shrubs suited to their local conditions. The Missouri Department of Conservation recommends American beautyberry, Virginia sweet-spire, Carolina allspice, New Jersey tea, wahoo, black chokeberry, fragrant sumac and ninebark. Heavenly bamboo’s history shows how a plant introduced for its appearance can become a management concern outside cultivation. Its ability to spread, the difficulty of controlling established growth and documented bird deaths linked to heavy berry consumption have led the Missouri Department of Conservation to recommend avoiding the plant in favour of suitable native alternatives.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Learning to read at 86 has changed my whole life'
articles.summary: Alan, from Southampton, learned to read through the charity Read Easy.
articles.body:
An 86-year-old man said learning to read has enabled him to read his and his wife's anniversary cards for the first time in 65 years.

Alan Hannay, from Southampton, learned to read through the charity Read Easy, which helps adults across the country who struggle with the skill many of us take for granted.

Hannay told BBC Radio Solent: "It's changed my whole life, my confidence, changed my family life and everything around me.

"It's one of the best experiences I've ever had in my life."

Hannay said he now reads every morning for about an hour and a half and goes to the class twice a week.

The charity said Hannay is an "inspiring example of determination and courage".

It said he asked his local library in Hythe, Southampton, about learning to read, which led him to the charity and his reading coach, Angie.

During his working life as a professional chauffeur, he relied on his memory to drive his clients around London, and at the age of 70 he attended evening classes to improve his reading.

However, he found the group situation difficult.

He decided to seek help when one of his great grandchildren asked him to read a story.

Read Easy says 2.4 million adults in England alone cannot read at all or struggle to read.

Hannay said for those who cannot read, the "first and most important thing is to admit to people around you that you're not able to do this".

"And once you've admitted that, then you can go and get some help, and the help is there," he added.

articles.title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
articles.summary: BBC News hears from users, dealers, prison and recovery workers as the country battles with a deadly new drug epidemic.
articles.body:
The BBC's Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raid

Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide

The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood.

"This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.

The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars.

"You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.

He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune.

We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.

Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape.

Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.

We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States.

At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over.

It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl.

The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added.

When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce."

Medetomidine is what he means. Like xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me.

They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat.

At the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma.

They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty.

One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life.

As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid.

"It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement.

Both in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose".

"In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers.

Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so.

"The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it."

Overdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds.

His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina.

That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine.

"The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements."

And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois.

I meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity.

Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means.

He told me that despite the latest efforts by the US government to target the cartels by declaring them terrorist groups and labelling fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction, his supply chain is as strong as ever.

When I ask him if the targeting of boats containing suspected traffickers by the Trump administration has made any difference, he replies that his product is still getting through from Mexico.

"If it doesn't go over the wall, it goes under the wall. If it doesn't go through the border, it comes through the top border. This game is about adaptability."

And when I asked what has changed in his business, his answer was clear.

"Synthetics. We haven't seen... what synthetics can do yet. It's not even the tip of the iceberg," he tells me.

Chicago's largest jail, one of the largest jails in America, is Cook County. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening.

"In 2023, all of a sudden we saw a spike in overdose deaths, but then hand in hand with that we saw, around persons that had either passed away or people we revived, paper all over the place," explains Sheriff Tom Dart, who runs the jail. "We were seeing paper that was being burned and all of this was completely novel."

The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures.

Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. It also showed them lighting paper in microwaves in the cell block kitchens.

It was indeed, as Dart said, a novel approach. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the pages of books and in letters.

"Cannabinoids and being soaked in a range of other things that were then subsequently lit on fire and inhaled to get high", the sheriff explained.

Cannabinoids, sometimes know as K2, are an entirely synthetic version of a cannabis plant extract. They are extremely dangerous and were to blame for the fatal seizures.

In August, I joined Dart's corrections officers as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. Around two dozen officers tread lightly and speak in hushed tones as they gather outside the block door. "Don't let them hear you. Silence, silence," commands one of the officers leading the search.

As the officers rush in, I smell burning paper in the air and can hear the sound of toilets flushing, presumably as contraband is hurriedly disposed of.

As the search gets under way, the focus is on any paper in the cells - the books and letters belonging to inmates.

The detainees are escorted to a holding area as the cells are turned over. Every scrap of paper in the rooms is checked by the officers. There are burn marks on the vents in many of the cells, where inmates place smoulder tapers that allow them to ignite the drug-soaked paper.

Now every piece of post that enters the jail is scanned for moisture. Somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters test positive and are rejected.

Outside the jail's walls, it's not hard to encounter the effects of the synthetic drugs wave on Chicago's streets. In the west of the city, day and night, men and women are bent double, swaying, as Mike did, as fentanyl and other synthetics surge through them.

In the upscale Oak Park neighbourhood, the local metro station has a vending machine that dispenses naloxone for free. Nearby, a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair has deep wounds in his legs, likely from xylazine use. He's being tended to by 40-year-old Karen Bell.

Karen is a recovery worker with the group Liv4Lali. A former heroin user, she's 17 years free from hard drugs.

She exudes kindness, and when I ask her about the drugs being used now, she says, "so many things are being mixed in right now. And it's affecting our bodies, whether it's the wounds, whether it's the withdrawals - and sometimes wounds can extend to the point where it's life changing."

Her organisation, like Hope Dealers in Columbus, distributes test strips which check drugs for fentanyl, medetomidine, xylazine and other adulterants.

The drugs now, says Karen, are "way more dangerous".

"Because before, back in my day, I stopped using heroin 17 years ago, right. That was still heroin. When you bought that you knew it was heroin. But now, when you buy a bag, you don't know really what it is," she tells me.

Dart has been sheriff of Cook County for 20 years, so I ask him how the war on drugs was progressing. "I don't think there's anybody involved with it who would sit there and say it's a raging success. It's not," he tells me.

And the new problem, he says, reiterating the Chicago drug dealer, is synthetics.

"The tradition has always been that law enforcement had an even more vital role because everything that was potent was coming across the border, whether it was coming from Colombia, Mexico, China, the poppy fields of Afghanistan. Now, with the explosion of synthetic drugs, people can do this in their house, in their sink, in their bathtub, you name it."

Victory in the war on drugs won't come from focusing just on the supply side, the sheriff adds. "Front and centre there's got to be huge substance abuse treatment," he says, mentioning a number of recovery programmes running in his jail.

"You can reduce the market if you can address people's issues with substance abuse. And I know many people who, after long struggles, have come out on the other side in a really good way."

Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby, now 17. After our meeting at the metro station, I meet them both in a country park in a suburb outside Chicago. With typical care, Karen tells me to watch out for the poison ivy as we walk along a muddy track.

It wasn't far from here, around 17 years ago, that she was at her lowest ebb.

As the wind blows through a tall oak tree beside us, she says: "The day I found out I was pregnant, I was on my way to commit suicide. I was so fed up with trying to quit. I was so fed up with living in a tent in the woods, using a bucket. I was so fed up with losing my friends and family because I was just so ashamed."

A pregnancy test changed her mind. She then spent time in Cook County jail for theft. Her parents, sensing an opportunity for her to get clean, refused to pay her bail money. So Karen got clean and Abby was born inside the jail.

When I ask Abby, who wants to become a tattoo artist, whether she's ever been tempted to experiment with drugs, she says: "Nah, I've seen it mess with my family too much, with my dad, my mum, killing my aunt, my uncles. You know, it's not worth it to get high for like a couple of hours."

She continues: "There's a lot of people are struggling, especially that our country is raising our prices, raising the prices on food and it's causing it. A lot of mental health now is very expensive so people can't get help, and one way they can turn to that is by drugs."

Generations of Americans have endured the drugs crisis, but it is never the same crisis. It has shifted from heroin, to prescription opioids to fentanyl and now to a whole new range of synthetics.

Successive administrations have fought - and lost - the war against drugs. The dealers, the suppliers, the cartels and users all adapt, always a few steps ahead of efforts to stop them.

articles.title: ‘This clearly reveals his intentions’: Uttrakhand minister Rekha Arya on husband’s demand to withdraw FIR
articles.summary: DEHRADUN: Uttarakhand Women Empowerment and Child Development minister Rekha Arya has dismissed her husband’s corruption allegations as “100 per cent
articles.body: DEHRADUN: Uttarakhand Women Empowerment and Child Development minister Rekha Arya has dismissed her husband’s corruption allegations as “100 per cent baseless”, saying her financial records are transparent and she is prepared to face an investigation.Arya’s response came a day after her husband, Girdhari Lal Sahu, released a video accusing her of possessing illegal assets worth Rs 210 crore and urging the chief minister to order an inquiry. He did not provide any documentary evidence to support his claims.The allegations came amid a police case registered against Sahu following a complaint by Arya, who has accused him of physical assault, harassment, caste-based slurs and death threats.Speaking on Saturday, Arya said the burden of proof lay with the person making the allegations.“My life is an open book. Everything is documented, including my income tax returns. I intend to contest future elections. I believe everything is transparent, and nothing is hidden. Nevertheless, if anyone harbours any doubts, they are free to initiate an investigation so that the truth can be brought to light,” she said.Sahu’s video, released on Friday, also questioned the authenticity of an audio recording shared by Arya on social media on Thursday evening. He alleged that the recording had been generated using artificial intelligence (AI) “to sow discord within the family” and dismissed the allegations against him as baseless.In the video, Sahu appealed to Arya to withdraw the FIR and retract her statements, maintaining that the accusations against him were false.Rejecting his claim that the recording was fabricated, Arya said, “I swear by my deity, Golju, that the audio is 100 per cent authentic. It has not been fabricated, nor was it created with the help of artificial intelligence."Responding to Sahu’s demand that she withdraw the police complaint, Arya said his position suggested that he believed the allegations would disappear if she withdrew the case.“Sahu-ji is saying that if I withdraw the complaint, all allegations will vanish. But if I do not withdraw it, the allegations will remain. This clearly reveals his intentions,” she said.‘Women should not endure atrocities’Arya also defended her decision to speak publicly about the allegations after filing the police complaint, saying women must raise their voices against domestic violence regardless of their social or professional standing.She said her political career began in 2003, when she was elected as an independent Zila Panchayat member with the support of her maternal family. She subsequently entered the Legislative Assembly and went on to become a minister.In his video, Sahu claimed that he had “elevated a woman found standing on the street to a position of prominence,” alleging that she had since forgotten his contribution because of the arrogance of her current position.Arya, meanwhile, said women should not remain silent when subjected to abuse.“Women should not endure atrocities; they must speak out against them. Only then will this come to an end," she said.The minister also thanked members of her party, opposition parties and the public for their support.SIT formed to investigate allegationsA nine-member Special Investigation Team (SIT) has been constituted to investigate Arya’s allegations against her husband, officials said.The FIR was registered at Dehradun’s Cantt police station on October 15 under relevant legal provisions, including three sections of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.Arya had also released a video on social media detailing her allegations against Sahu. Following the complaint, her health deteriorated and she was hospitalised.The SIT is tasked with investigating the allegations of physical assault, harassment, caste-based slurs and death threats levelled by the minister against her husband.Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news.
