articles.title: There is no split in MAGA
articles.summary: But there is an attempt to redefine who the movement includes and what it stands for.
articles.body:
As the midterm elections near, we are hearing a lot about a “split” within the Make America Great Again (MAGA) coalition, which got Donald Trump elected United States president in 2024. I understand the tragedy of MAGA a little differently: not as a split, but as a refusal by the best members of that coalition to abandon the solidarity we’ve formed between us.

I had the privilege of helping bring this coalition together in 2024. It was a collection of groupings traditionally pitted against each other: social conservatives, pro-lifers, devout Christians, devout Muslims, devout Quakers, disaffected leftists, young first-time voters – all coming together behind a Republican candidacy.

Together, we made history and delivered a moral mandate based on a humane concern for the human cost of unregulated borders, thoughtless warmongering overseas and the ruling-class politicking that had allowed a Jeffrey Epstein syndicate to go unpunished while the basic dignity of the “least of our brethren” went untended.

In the campaign’s final stretch, I visited Syrian Christian churches in Pennsylvania and met Americans whose families had personally suffered the worst of what Washington’s foreign policy can do. In those communities, we talked about Gaza, peace and Trump’s promises .

This miraculous, ragtag, all-American patchwork of people who supported Trump in 2024 truly became a people when they discovered their shared belief in the mission of electing a president who would break with the Washington establishment’s inhumane policies.

Today, that coalition is remarkably intact. What is instead happening is that there is a concerted effort to redefine what MAGA is.

In the weeks following the launch of the disastrous US-Israeli war on Iran, Trump announced “I am MAGA” and insisted on including in the brand the ideology of infamous neo-cons like Mark Levin.

As a result, MAGA has now become a blunt instrument of the same war-hungry elites the original coalition aimed to depose. The brand is now on course to be destroyed this November. That, however, says nothing about the goodness and power of the movement that stood behind Trump in 2024.

Perhaps one of the central factors that is driving this process of MAGA destruction is the decision to support, fund and protect Israel at any cost as it carries out a genocide in Gaza and various other atrocities in the Middle East.

And Election Day 2026 will represent the first time the public’s moral indignation fully makes itself felt. But, bafflingly, that’s also the one matter that our most powerful politicians have made a point of doubling down on ahead of the midterms.

Just a few days ago, The New York Times reported that David Milstein, senior adviser to US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee and stepson of Levin, repeatedly suppressed or rewrote embassy reporting on Israeli violence against Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank. Milstein allegedly even blocked reporting about the killings of Palestinian Americans by Israeli settlers and security forces. Nevertheless, he still retains his position.

I write this as an American conservative and a Catholic. But at a time when Washington is spending America’s moral authority to shield Israel’s government from accountability while treating Palestinian lives as negotiable, both my deepest-held convictions and my patriotism require that I stand against some of the loudest self-proclaimed “patriots” and “conservative Christians”. Not because I now reject what they claim to represent, but because I still embrace it.

An April survey by Pew Research found that 57 percent of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents aged 18 to 49 viewed Israel unfavourably. Young conservatives have watched the same harrowing footage of the Gaza genocide as everyone else. Today’s new self-proclaimed leaders of MAGA – a movement that taught the youth to distrust official narratives – cannot reasonably expect them to stop asking questions.

Especially not when there are still plenty of prominent figures who have retained their integrity and still carry the original coalition’s banner.

Trump’s former counterterrorism chief Joe Kent courageously resigned over the Iran war and publicly described the Israeli and lobbying pressure that helped bring it about. Former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard bravely put on record that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon and had not rebuilt its enrichment capability since the 12-day war of 2025, undercutting the “imminent nuclear threat” claim used to justify the war this year.

Former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene and Congressman Thomas Massie stood against the Gaza genocide and the Epstein cover-up. Trump and the donor-class backers of his newly adopted neo-con agenda pummelled them: Greene resigned, and Massie lost his primary after a multimillion-dollar campaign to unseat him.

Conservative activist Carrie Prejean Boller defended Christian opposition to Israel’s violence in Gaza and the bigoted ideology of Zionism. She paid a price, losing her seat on Trump’s Religious Liberty Commission, but proved herself a true leader in our movement.

Conservative commentators Tucker Carlson and Alex Jones similarly used their influential platforms to stand up to Trump over the Iran war and against US backing of Israeli abuses of Palestinians.

And consider the comedians and podcasters: Joe Rogan, Theo Von, Tim Dillon and others. Trump’s son Barron was credited with the brilliant idea of bringing his father’s campaign to their audiences in 2024. They graciously opened their platforms: Rogan endorsed Trump, Von interviewed him and Dillon hosted JD Vance after he became the vice presidential nominee.

Now these same voices are condemning the bloodshed and broken promises. From Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank to Iran, Trump has squandered their goodwill.

These political and cultural leaders represent a preview of the future this coalition still has ahead of it. The candidates they eventually support – or themselves, if they run – will be easily recognisable to voters. And I and millions of others will be behind them.

Browbeating the voters whose support the Trump administration betrayed will have exactly the consequences you would expect. The original MAGA coalition will destroy a Republican Party that embraces the policies the movement aimed to destroy all along. On Election Day, the coalition’s moral indignation will fully make itself felt.

Don’t be misled by talk of a “split” in our movement. When the new “MAGA” falls, it will not be due to a disintegration of our coalition. It will be because our coalition is still going strong.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Novak Djokovic joins a $126 billion investment firm as global strategic advisor, building on his startup bets and expanding his business interests beyond tennis
articles.summary: Novak Djokovic is expanding his business interests by joining General Atlantic, a global investment firm managing billions.
articles.body: Novak Djokovic is expanding his business interests by joining General Atlantic, a global investment firm managing billions. The appointment adds a new dimension to the Serbian tennis champion’s activities beyond the court, building on his experience backing startups and exploring investment opportunities. Rather than taking charge of the firm’s funds, Djokovic will bring his perspective to an established investment network while continuing his professional tennis career. The move comes as elite athletes increasingly look towards venture capital and business partnerships to build opportunities beyond competition, creating a longer-term role in the commercial world.Djokovic takes on an advisory role at General AtlanticGeneral Atlantic, headquartered in New York, invests in businesses across several sectors and operates internationally. As Global Strategic Advisor, Djokovic will work with General Atlantic’s leadership, portfolio companies and investors, contributing perspectives drawn from elite sport, entrepreneurship and investing. The firm’s announcement does not specify whether his responsibilities will extend to individual investment decisions or fund management.The role marks a more formal step into the financial world for a sportsman whose commercial activities have extended beyond endorsements and sponsorship agreements. His experience as an elite athlete is part of the connection he has drawn between professional sport and investing, particularly in areas such as planning, leadership and working towards long-term objectives.Speaking to ABC News on 25 June, Djokovic discussed the similarities he sees between the two fields. His comments came just days before Wimbledon began, with the tournament providing the immediate backdrop to the announcement. The appointment itself, however, points to interests that extend beyond the demands of the tennis calendar.From backing startups to a wider investment roleDjokovic has previously backed startups and developed business interests outside professional tennis. His move to General Atlantic builds on that experience, bringing him closer to an established investment firm rather than leaving his involvement with businesses limited to individual ventures.The specific investments Djokovic has made, and the extent of his responsibilities at General Atlantic, should be distinguished from the broader announcement of his advisory appointment. General Atlantic's investment operations are separate from Djokovic's role as an adviser. The announcement instead establishes a professional connection between the tennis champion and a major participant in global private investment.Wimbledon remains a major part of Djokovic's careerThe business announcement arrived as Djokovic prepared for the 2026 Wimbledon Championships, which began on 29 June. He entered the tournament with seven Wimbledon singles titles and the prospect of matching Roger Federer's record of eight men's singles championships.In his interview with ABC News, Djokovic spoke about the significance the tournament has held for him since childhood. Wimbledon has long been one of the defining events of his career, and his pursuit of another title remains a separate undertaking from his growing involvement in business.His record at the tournament includes the 2019 final against Federer, which Djokovic won in five sets after a deciding-set tie-break. The match remains one of the most memorable encounters in the competition's history. It also illustrates the level of sustained performance required to remain a contender at the top of men's tennis over many years.For Djokovic, the immediate challenge is still competition. His appointment at General Atlantic offers another professional direction, but it does not signal an announced retirement from the sport or a move away from the tour.Building a professional life beyond tennisA career at the highest level of tennis comes with a finite competitive window, even for players who remain successful well into their thirties. Business investments and advisory positions can provide athletes with experience and relationships that develop on a different timetable from their sporting achievements.Djokovic's new role gives him an opportunity to participate in the work of a global investment firm while continuing to compete. How extensively he becomes involved in its activities, or whether the position leads to further investment ventures, has not been detailed in the announcement.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fighting intensifies across Yemen as humanitarian crisis deepens
articles.summary: Clashes between Yemeni forces and Houthis cause casualties on both sides as aid agencies warn of humanitarian crisis.
articles.body:
Fighting between government forces and Houthi fighters has intensified across multiple fronts in Yemen amid a spiralling humanitarian crisis.

Eight soldiers loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government were killed during heavy clashes on the al-Maqatirah front in Lahij governorate, the government-affiliated Tur al-Bahah military axis said in a statement on Saturday.

In Taiz governorate, government troops said they killed 12 Houthi fighters in al-Aqroud, following days of fighting on the outskirts of Taiz city, where Saudi Arabia-backed government forces reported repelling Houthi advances and inflicting heavy losses on the group.

Elsewhere in Taiz, government forces said they broke a Houthi attack on the al-Shaqab front, while government-aligned Homeland Shield Forces reported destroying a Houthi supply vehicle with a drone in al-Wazziyah. The Southern Giants Brigades also said they targeted Houthi positions with precision strikes in al-Madaribah, near the Lahij border.

Meanwhile, government troops and allied Popular Resistance fighters pressed ahead with their offensive in al-Jawf and Marib.

Military officials reported using artillery barrages and drone strikes against Houthi military positions, barracks and troop assemblies in al-Jawf, while coalition aircraft bombed Houthi command hubs and supply depots.

Government artillery and missile units also targeted Houthi lines in Marib.

Yemen’s war has escalated sharply since the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the country’s internationally recognised government along the Red Sea coast last month.

Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded to the losses with a counteroffensive, and then launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, seized by the Iran-aligned group in 2014.

On the aerial front, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed that the group’s air defence forces brought down a Saudi reconnaissance drone over the governorate of Hajjah. He identified the aircraft as a Turkish-manufactured Lentatek Karayel drone, saying it was the fourth of its kind downed since the latest escalation began.

The Houthis also claimed they shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter in the kingdom’s border province of Najran.

Saudi-led coalition spokesman Colonel Turki al-Maliki said an AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter had crashed in Najran due to a technical malfunction, killing two crew members.

Houthi media also reported 10 Saudi air strikes targeting sites in Saada governorate.

Off the coast of al-Mukalla, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency reported that at least seven armed men on board a skiff attacked a liquefied natural gas (LNG) tanker. They fired two shots at the tanker before the vessel’s onboard security detail returned two warning shots, forcing the attackers to change course and disengage.

Meanwhile, the human cost of the conflict continues to rise, with humanitarian agencies warning of worsening conditions for civilians.

According to the International Organization for Migration, more than 233,000 people have been displaced since fighting escalated in Yemen, including about 121,000 in Taiz governorate alone.

The World Health Organization has also warned that Taiz city has become functionally isolated, with its 12 hospitals holding fuel for only four days, no surgical supplies, and facing critical shortages of oxygen and medicine amid a growing cholera outbreak.

The displacement crisis has spread to East Africa, with the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) confirming that more than 4,000 refugees have reached the region — 3,800 in Djibouti and roughly 200 in Somalia. The UNHCR also reported that health workers are treating a cholera outbreak at Djibouti’s Markazi camp, where 31 cases and one death have been recorded.

articles.title: Funding for new Sunderland musical history project
articles.summary: Sunderland Music City has been awarded more than £150,000 for its Mackem Music Memories project.
articles.body:
A major new heritage project has been awarded funding to preserve Sunderland's musical history.

Sunderland Music City has been awarded more than £150,000 by the National Lottery Heritage Fund for its Mackem Music Memories project.

The organisation, that aims to deliver economic, employment, cultural and social benefits through music, is inviting residents of the city past and present to contribute their memories of the music scene to be used in an exhibition.

Music City's chief executive Michelle Daurat said she hoped the project would "become part of Sunderland's permanent heritage."

£156,166 has been awarded by the National Heritage Lottery Fund and will be used to gather stories of people's most memorable musical moments.

Music City hopes to gather more than 300 memories through questionnaires, community research and interviews.

"This project is about much more than looking backwards," Daurat said.

"It is about understanding where our music city came from, celebrating the people who made it what it is today, and inspiring the musicians and communities who will shape its future."

Sunderland became the second UK city to join the Music Cities Network in 2025. The global organisation helps cities grow their music sector and supports cultural, social and economic development through education, rehearsal and recording spaces, and fostering a live music scene.

Since joining the network, live music venues in Sunderland reported an increase in footfall and the city hosted Radio 1's Big Weekend in May 2026.

The memories will be displayed in an exhibition at the newly-opened Culture House Sunderland in summer 2027, alongside a programme of community activity, live events, digital archiving and musical heritage trails.

Music City says that Mackem Music Memories will also reflect the city as it is today, and will work with South Asian, Filipino, Nigerian and Eastern European communities, as well as the city's international student population.

After its close in December 2027, the exhibition and research will be digitised and incorporated into the Sunderland Local Studies Collection.

Daurat continued: "Sunderland's musical heritage is written in its people. We are delighted that The National Lottery Heritage Fund is supporting us to capture those stories before they disappear and to make sure they become part of Sunderland's permanent heritage."

Anyone wishing to contribute their musical memories can do so via an online questionnaire .

articles.title: Food or medicine? The impossible choices facing Sudan’s chronically ill
articles.summary: Sudanese are facing growing costs of medicine caused by the country’s civil war.
articles.body:
Hasanat al-Rashid, 48, has lived with diabetes for 15 years, and the three-and-a-half-year civil war between Sudan’s military and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group has worsened her situation. Finding the treatment she needs has become a daily struggle.

When the war broke out in April 2023, she was forced to flee south from her home in Haj Yousif in Khartoum North to Umm Daw Ban in Khartoum State.

During her displacement, she went for days without medication and was forced to eat foods unsuitable for her condition, such as asida , a traditional Sudanese porridge.

She underwent operations on her foot twice when she developed complications of diabetes, including a severe infection.

She moved between hospitals in Gezira State south of Khartoum, seeking treatment in Rufaa, Wad Madani and Al-Hasahisa. When fighting spread to these areas in December 2023, she fled again, arriving in Port Sudan, a city on the Red Sea that was less affected by the war.

Her condition has worsened to the point that she now has to use insulin every day and with this comes added costs, something that forces diabetes sufferers in Sudan to choose between medicine and other essentials, such as food.

“The doses vary depending on whether my blood sugar is high or low,” she told Al Jazeera.

The war has pushed income levels in Sudan back to those last seen in the 1990s, according to the United Nations Development Programme. This means Hasanat and other diabetes sufferers are struggling to afford the medicine they need to treat the condition.

Hasanat’s doctor recommended she use an insulin pen, a device used to inject insulin under the skin. She would need one or two of the devices a month, but the cost at 70,000 Sudanese pounds ($8) is more than she can afford up front, so she opts for a vial of insulin.

This is cheaper at 17,000 Sudanese pounds ($1.80), but there is the additional cost of buying ice every day to keep the insulin cool. She spends 180,000 pounds ($20) a month on ice to preserve the medicine. But she is able to spread these costs out through the month, making the vials her only viable option even if the overall costs are higher than an insulin pen.

“It may last a month or less, but the challenge is that I don’t have a refrigerator, so I struggle to store the insulin properly,” she said.

She also needs painkillers and vitamins on a regular basis to manage complications caused by the diabetes.

Fatima Adam, 75, is among the patients at Port Sudan Hospital struggling to afford the medicines she needs to manage her hypertension and a thyroid condition.

She was admitted to the hospital with complications caused by high blood pressure, which has started to impact her heart. Too unwell to speak to Al Jazeera herself, her daughter, Aisha, described how the rising cost of treatment has affected her whole family.

Before the war, Fatima received medicine through the National Health Insurance Fund. She paid a quarter of the cost while the fund covered the rest. But when the war started and the economy collapsed , the medicines she needed were no longer covered by the scheme.

“My mother takes six different medicines because hypertension has affected her heart in addition to her thyroid medication. The war has made things harder because the prices of these medicines have gone up,” Aisha told Al Jazeera.

The responsibility for paying for Fatima’s treatment and supporting her and her daughter falls on her son, who works as a casual worker. With no fixed income, he goes to the market every day in search of work but sometimes returns home empty without any luck.

“Sometimes, when my brother finds work, we buy enough medicine to last a month. Other times, we have to buy smaller quantities and take the medicines intermittently,” Aisha said.

She bought a month’s supply of her mother’s medication a few days ago for 160,000 Sudanese pounds ($17.80), a substantial expense for a family whose income depends on day labour but essential to treating Fatima’s condition.

The war has caused an estimated $500m in losses to medicine stocks, infrastructure and transport fleets, dealing a major blow to Sudan’s pharmaceutical supply system, the National Medical Supplies Fund told Al Jazeera.

The National Medicines and Poisons Board estimated that only eight of the 30 pharmaceutical factories in Khartoum that shut down during the conflict have resumed operations despite the security situation in the capital recently improving.

This has increased Sudan’s reliance on imported medicines, but the subsequent depreciation of the Sudanese pound has driven up the costs of pharmaceutical procurement and production.

Hossam al-Naeem, who works as a pharmacist in Port Sudan, said customers with diabetes and hypertension require regular painkillers and vitamins to help their overall condition.

“I feel deeply saddened when I see the expressions on some patients’ faces as they ask about the prices of medicines and discover how much they have increased because of the depreciation of the Sudanese pound,” Hossam told Al Jazeera.

The currency’s collapse has created added challenges for pharmacists. Before the war, a dollar traded for roughly 600 Sudanese pounds. Now black-market currency traders are quoting rates of 9,300 pounds to the dollar, meaning higher costs for most goods in Sudan.

Sometimes Hossam incurs losses himself when he finds that the prices of drugs have risen sharply, and keeping essential medicines stocked is becoming difficult.

“I used to sell a strip of cold and flu tablets for 6,000 Sudanese pounds [70 cents]. But when I went to buy new stock, I found that the supplier’s price was also 6,000 pounds per strip. That means I made no profit, not even enough to cover the pharmacy’s operating costs,” he said.

Huda Mahmoud, 58, lives in el-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state in south-central Sudan, where drone attacks and other violence remain a problem while the military is making advances towards the city.

Huda has lived with heart problems for more than 12 years and described the impacts of the war as being physical, financial and emotional.

“I take five different medicines. There was a time when they weren’t available, and I suffered a lot. Sometimes, I had to ask people in Wad Madani, Sennar or Port Sudan to send them to me,” she told Al Jazeera. “The medicines were extremely expensive, costing me 300,000 Sudanese pounds [$33.30] a month.”

Taking medication has become a carefully managed routine with each pill tied to a specific time of day.

“I’ve become tied to my pills: this one before eating, that one afterwards. If I forget one, my heart starts beating very fast,” she added.

In March, Huda was forced to travel from el-Obeid to Omdurman. Following her strict treatment regimen has become increasingly difficult during repeated periods of upheaval.

She has now returned home to el-Obeid, where her regular medicine is priced at 151,000 Sudanese pounds ($16.80) a month, something she can barely afford.

Her greatest fear is running out of medicine or being unable to afford her next supply, which would put her at risk of a blood clot.

“I’m afraid of becoming incapacitated. I used to be responsible for the whole household, but now I need help. I feel like I’ve become a burden on my family,” she said.

articles.title: In Wyoming, an automated camera system detected approaching eagles and triggered turbine shutdowns; an initial study estimated 82% lower fatalities than at a control site
articles.summary: A groundbreaking automated camera system in Wyoming has led to an 82% reduction in eagle fatalities at wind turbines, highlighting the potential for technology to protect wildlife while harnessing renewable energy.
articles.body: Wind power and eagles both depend on open, windy land. Large raptors such as golden eagles use steady winds and rising air currents to travel and hunt with little effort and wind developers site turbines on ridges and plains for the same conditions. This spatial overlap places eagles within range of the moving blades and has long complicated wildlife management and turbine permitting operations. Operators either shut down turbines temporarily or slow them when birds are detected, generally with the help of on-site human observers. Observers could monitor only a limited number of turbines and could not remain active all day. This prompted research into whether cameras and software could do the job without human direction. A case study conducted in Wyoming tested this idea.How IdentiFlight works at Top of the WorldThe Peregrine Fund describes IdentiFlight as a combination of camera and machine learning technology that detects flying objects, classifies them and shuts down the turbine if an eagle is threatened with impact. In a 2021 study published in the Journal of Applied Ecology, Christopher J. W. McClure, Brian W. Rolek, Leah Dunn, Jennifer D. McCabe, Luke Martinson and Todd E. Katzner evaluated an automated camera system designed to detect approaching eagles and stop wind turbines at the Top of the World Windpower facility in Wyoming. The researchers compared eagle fatalities at the facility with those at a nearby control site. The above-mentioned study found that estimated eagle fatalities at the treatment site declined by 63% between the periods before and after automated curtailment was introduced, while fatalities at the control site increased by 113%.The January 2021 before-after-control-impact studyThe findings were published on January 20, 2021, in the Journal of Applied Ecology in a paper titled Eagle fatalities are reduced by automated curtailment of wind turbines, available through the US Geological Survey (USGS) publication page. The researchers used a before-after-control-impact experimental design. They compared eagle fatality rates at Top of the World with those at a control location 15 km away, which lacked automated curtailment, both before and after the implementation of the automated system. A control location is important because eagle abundance and weather conditions change annually.The 82% lower fatality rateThe USGS summary of the study explained that the team corrected for carcass detection probability using the GenEst software and scaled fatality estimates to turbine-years, which is why the comparison was framed as a rate rather than a raw count. After those modifications, the team concluded that the mortality rate at the treatment site was 82% lower than at the control site. The summary also noted that the technology does not eliminate all collisions and that the authors viewed automated curtailment as promising but not a standalone fix, saying its effectiveness could improve when paired with other mitigation measures. The 2023 USGS reanalysis: 50%, from -159% to 89%A later 2023 paper in the Journal of Applied Ecology, Reanalysis indicates little evidence of reduction in eagle mortality rate by automated curtailment of wind turbines, was written by USGS scientists Manuela Huso and Daniel Dalthorp. The reanalysis examined the same treatment site over roughly four years before IdentiFlight was installed and only about six months to one year afterwards, alongside a control site and argued that the data do not support a clear change in underlying mortality rate. The authors concluded that the effect estimate was too imprecise to rule out either a decrease or an increase.There were four problems that Huso and Dalthorp found with this data. First, the original study compared the mean of four years before activation with just one year after, without controlling for year-to-year variation. Also, there was only one treatment year at one location, which is insufficient to establish a causal effect. The effect size was exaggerated because it assumed the deviation at the neighboring site would also apply to the treatment site, and it varied depending on the arbitrary date used to divide the before and after periods. Lastly, 7 of 42 reported eagle fatalities were left out of the analysis and the reason was unclear. With these corrections in mind, the USGS note provides an estimate of a 50% reduction with an interval from -159% to 89%, a range that includes no reduction or even an increase.What remains open: more years at more sitesThe 2023 authors did not claim that automated curtailment cannot benefit eagles. They wrote that it has obvious potential in theory, but that the Wyoming results do not support the overly optimistic effect size and precision first reported. The authors added that evaluating the technology and informing management decisions will require several more years of data from multiple locations. For the wind industry and regulators, the Wyoming results should be treated as inconclusive: the technology’s potential is plausible in theory, but the data have not yet demonstrated it. Replication across multiple sites and years is still needed before automated shutdown systems can be considered a well-supported solution to eagle fatalities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Florida fisherman, 71, killed by nearly 12-foot alligator as rescuers face more gators
articles.summary: Steven Hamilton was fishing at Lake Apopka in Winter Garden, Florida, when he was attacked in the second fatal alligator incident in the state this year.
articles.body: A 71-year-old man was killed Friday by a nearly 12-foot alligator in the second fatal attack in Florida this year, police said. Steven Hamilton was fishing along the shore of Lake Apopka in Winter Garden near Orlando, when he was attacked around 5 p.m., the Winter Garden Police Department said. Emergency crews attempted to rescue Hamilton, but weren’t able to because other alligators were also in the water, Winter Garden Fire Chief Jose Gainza told FOX 35. SON OF FLORIDA ALLIGATOR ATTACK VICTIM SAYS TOURISTS AND TIKTOKERS ARE EMBOLDENING THE GATORS The alligator was trapped and killed, Winter Garden Police Chief Michael Mason said. Mason said the lake "has tons of alligators in it" and authorities weren’t aware before the attack that one was near the shore. It looks like it's docile, it looks like your Florida emblem, but it can be dangerous." American alligators can be found all over Florida, although attacks are rare. In June, a 31-year-old woman named Brittany Clark was killed by an alligator near her home in Oviedo. articles.title: To keep the Panama Canal flowing, the living and the dead must pay the price
articles.summary: The Panama Canal’s Rio Indio reservoir project is expected to flood dozens of communities, requiring families to relocate — along with their deceased loved ones.
articles.body: When Maricel Sánchez’s family buried her grandmother 15 years ago, she never expected she would have to dig her back up one day. But that’s the morbid situation she faces due to plans by the Panama Canal Authority to build a new reservoir that will feed the crucial waterway that handles about 5% of the world’s shipping. The canal authority — an autonomous government agency — says the Rio Indio reservoir project is essential to keep the waterway functioning because the impacts of fossil fuel pollution and El Niño, a natural climate pattern, have made this area of central Panama increasingly prone to droughts. To make way for what will be the third reservoir to serve the canal, an area of more than 11,000 acres that is currently home to schools, churches, farms and cemeteries will have to be flooded and at least 1,600 residents re-homed. That will upend the lives of locals like 27-year-old Sánchez and her two young daughters, whose rural town of Limón de Chagres is one of dozens of communities along the Indio River that will be affected. The cemetery where her family members are buried is one of eight in the flood zone that will have to be exhumed. “This took me completely by surprise,” Sánchez said. “I never imagined they would dare to interfere with something so sensitive to us as rural people.” The canal authority has said that relocating the remains will be coordinated in advance with family members, with respect for religious beliefs, cultural sensitivities and emotional ties. Local authorities will cover the cost of the whole process — from new coffins or urns to headstones at the new sites. But many residents say there’s no humane way to carry out an exhumation, especially on ancestral lands where more than five generations are buried. “It is hard enough to endure the pain of losing a family member, but I feel that when they dig them up again, you re-live that pain all over again,” Sánchez said. A government decree ended burials at El Limón cemetery in July. The seven other cemeteries will become off-limits for burials in January 2027. Construction on the reservoir is expected to begin in 2028 with the project slated for completion between 2031 and 2032. The canal authority says that, when completed, the new reservoir will both boost its operations by 10 to 15% and help supply water to nearby communities. “It represents a significant step towards canal sustainability, reliability, and competitiveness, for the benefit of all Panamanians and global trade,” the ACP said in February last year, while pledging to set aside funds for compensating, resettling and supporting families and property owners. However, many locals are skeptical of how much compensation they will receive — if any at all. They have also raised fears over whether farming and fishing communities will be able to sustain themselves. ‘We are not objects to be moved around’ Olegario Cedeño Rojas, 40, a farmer in Limón de Chagres, is among those skeptics. All four of his grandparents are buried in El Limón cemetery. Exhuming them, he says, means reliving the pain of losing them. And losing his land means losing the foundation of his life, he told CNN. “How can they compensate me with something permanent — something enduring — when I am giving up my land, my life, and everything I have?” he asked. “The land is our life insurance — our only permanent, enduring asset of value and the sole source of livelihood for all of us farmers.” For most people, farming, fishing and river transport are all they know. While farmers fear the land they’re relocated to will be less fertile, workers in river transport — such as Sánchez, who boats people up and down the Indio — fear the project could limit their access to the water. Fishermen, too, have reason to worry. Experts warn that the dam needed to create the reservoir will disrupt the river’s natural flow, to the detriment of marine life. LeRoy Poff, biology professor at Colorado State University and a river ecology expert, says fish species moving up and down the river to reproduce will be hindered by the dam, dealing a blow to a vital source of food and income for locals and downstream communities. The socio-environmental manager of the reservoir project, Karina Vergara, told CNN that the areas to be resettled were nearby and would have similar soil and conditions favorable to farming. However, she admitted the land had not yet been formally acquired, saying the authority was still negotiating with the current owners and that some of the areas still needed infrastructure such as roads. Asked to put a date on the resettlements, she said there was no specific timeline because the canal was committed to “doing this process gradually and carefully, working with the people.” But she said resettlement was still slated for sometime in 2027 and that the first relocations would be to areas where basic infrastructure such as houses, schools and roads were already in place. For many residents, uncertainties over the timeline have only added to their anxiety, while experts say the whole process seems far behind schedule. “I would think that at this point they would at least have relocation sites and would start recreating farms,” said Osvaldo Jordan, CEO of wetlands conservation organization CREHO. Sánchez, meanwhile, says the process hasn’t been as mutual and collaborative as authorities make it seem. “They make decisions about us as if we were mere objects,” Sánchez said. “We are not objects to be moved around.” A matter of climate and security Relocating populations to make way for dams is far from unprecedented in the region — though the practice often proves controversial. Similar debates were sparked by the building of Brazil’s Belo Monte dam, inaugurated in 2016, which displaced more than 40,000 people; and Colombia’s El Quimbo dam, on which construction began in 2011. In the case of El Quimbo, the Colombian government handed over land to 94 displaced families in 2024, but some campaigners estimate the true number of people affected runs into the hundreds or even thousands. Back on the Indio River, Panama appears to have calculated that any such controversy is outweighed by the importance of the project, which it has deemed a “top priority for national water security,” and its need to protect the canal — which contributes an estimated 8% of the country’s total annual GDP. Panama has a traditionally dry season that spans January to March, and a traditionally wet season from May to November, according to the country’s meteorology institute. The growing impacts of both natural El Niño patterns and man-made climate change are forcing the decision to build the new reservoir, officials say, because the country needs to store additional water during unusually wet dry seasons so it can be used when wet seasons turn out to be unusually dry. January to March of this year saw the area’s wettest dry season on record, said Steve Paton, director of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute’s Physical Monitoring Program in Panama. That was soon followed by the driest April-to-July period ever, according to Paton, who said the effects were “almost certainly the result of El Niño making itself felt.” ‘Are we going to end up underwater?’ Still, while the canal authority insists the reservoir is “for the benefit all Panamanians and global trade,” for many locals along the Indio River it is hard to see past the more immediate effects it will have on their daily lives. Alongside their fears over relocation and livelihoods, the expected disruptions to the flow of the river have raised doubts about whether the Indio can continue to be used as a transport route connecting many small villages and communities. Northwest of Limón de Chagres is El Jobo de Rio Indio, where Alexis Rodriguez grew up and still visits. He’s been living in Panama City for about a decade and travels the Indio River by boat for his trips back. Uncertainty over the dam’s effects have left him wondering how he will be able to visit his 91-year-old grandfather who raised him. Like Sánchez and Cedeño Rojas, he has loved ones buried in a cemetery slated for relocation. His great-grandparents have been there for 30 years, and other ancestors, even longer. “Having to open (the grave sites) up again and remove a loved one from there … it is very sad, painful and deeply shocking,” he said. For Sánchez, the new reservoir threatens to uproot not only generations past, but her daughters’ futures. Her 7-year-old hears the conversations around her, sees the protests in her community and notices the visiting canal personnel. “Mom, are they really going to flood us with water? Are we going to end up underwater?” she asks. “Where are we going to move?” But without the answer from authorities, Sanchez wonders: “How are we, as adults, supposed to give it to our children?”

articles.title: Google Maps route likely led truck to Gwalior temple, brakes failed before crash: CSP
articles.summary: GWALIOR: The truck that ploughed into devotees at the Sheetla Mata Temple fair in Gwalior, killing at least 15 people and injuring 26, may have taken a
articles.body: GWALIOR: The truck that ploughed into devotees at the Sheetla Mata Temple fair in Gwalior, killing at least 15 people and injuring 26, may have taken a shorter route suggested by Google Maps before its brakes failed, CSP Ravi Bhadoria told news agency ANI.The truck driver and owner have been taken into custody, he added.According to Bhadoria, the truck was carrying paddy from Debra Mandi. Since the drivers were unfamiliar with the area, they may have checked the location on Google Maps and taken a shorter route that led them towards the temple.“The brakes failed before the temple and this accident occurred,” Bhadoria said, adding that heavy vehicles had not previously used the route.Probe ordered into how truck reached restricted stretchBhadoria said parking arrangements, checkpoints and barricades were in place along the route, which was not meant for heavy vehicles. Senior officials have ordered an investigation into how the truck reached the stretch despite these measures.The accident took place around 1.30am on Sunday, when a large number of devotees had gathered at the temple for the Sharadiya Navratri fair.The truck ploughed into people near the shrine, killing at least 15 and injuring 26 others, including two police personnel. Two Home Guard jawans posted at the entry point were among those killed.The circumstances leading to the crash remain under investigation. While some accounts suggest the truck rolled down a slope after its brakes failed, questions have also been raised over how heavy vehicles entered a route closed to traffic during the festival.CSP removed, eight police personnel suspendedFollowing the accident, Madhya Pradesh chief minister Mohan Yadav removed Jhansi Road CSP Ravi Bhadoria and suspended eight other police personnel over alleged negligence.The truck's owner, Mohit Singh, and driver, Dilbag Singh, were arrested in Dholpur, police said. They are being questioned in connection with the incident.The state government has announced compensation of Rs 4 lakh for the families of those killed, Rs 2 lakh for each seriously injured person and Rs 50,000 for other injured people. We hope to make celebrations even more special this Diwali with our exciting offers across our Bespoke AI range of appliances," said Ghufran Alam, Vice President and Head of Digital Appliances Business, Samsung India.Samsung highlighted a range of AI-powered features available across its Bespoke AI portfolio. The company's Family Hub refrigerator now incorporates Generative AI capabilities and expanded food recognition features, including the ability to identify a larger variety of food items. According to Samsung, the AI Food Manager can track refrigerator inventory in real time, suggest recipes through SmartThings Food, provide step-by-step cooking assistance, manage shopping lists and alert users about food nearing expiry.The appliances are integrated with Samsung's SmartThings ecosystem and protected by Knox Security, which the company says provides enterprise-grade data protection.Offers available till November 15The festive offers are available through Samsung's official website, major e-commerce platforms and retail stores across India until November 15, 2026. articles.title: Egypt to provide ‘necessary’ support to Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
articles.summary: Presidency says Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with support to defend its security and protect its resources.
articles.body:
Egypt says it is ready to provide “all necessary and possible support to Saudi Arabia to defend its safety and stability”, as Yemen’s Houthi rebels continue to launch attacks on the kingdom.

The National Defence Council, chaired by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, said on Sunday that Egypt “stands fully with” Saudi Arabia to defend its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites.

The president’s office added that Cairo would also intensify diplomatic efforts for de-escalation.

The Iran-aligned Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have in recent days attacked Riyadh’s international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting in Yemen with forces loyal to the Saudi-backed, internationally ‌recognised government following the collapse of a truce.

Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would ⁠act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited ⁠Egypt last month after fighting in Yemen ⁠reignited.

He had also called for an emergency parliamentary session to authorise him to approve any requests from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance, if Riyadh were to ask.

Egypt’s House of Representatives is holding a plenary session on Sunday following the president’s call.

In last month’s Cairo meeting with the Saudi Crown Prince, Sisi had backed Saudi calls for secure and unhindered navigation in the Red Sea.

A statement from the Egyptian presidency at the time said that “the security of Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states is an integral part of Egypt’s national security”.

Analysts say Riyadh is looking for help to protect the kingdom and Red Sea shipping and that Egypt, whose Suez Canal revenue depends on the same traffic, is an obvious partner .

They say Egypt is eager to prevent Iran and its allies from imposing control over the region, especially over maritime traffic in the Red Sea, given the direct repercussions for the Suez Canal.

Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging Houthi attacks against the kingdom, a claim Tehran rejects.

articles.title: MIKE DAVIS: Justice Department must be wrapping up Rep. Ilhan Omar's Christmas present
articles.summary: The federal warrant for Ilhan Omar's DC home raid was reportedly signed by a judge who donated to Hillary Clinton, undermining claims of political revenge.
articles.body: When U.S. Department of Homeland Security agents raided the DC home of far-left Islamist and Democrat U.S. House Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota last Monday, they came armed with a judicial warrant. Omar’s fellow leftists shrieked that the raid amounted to political revenge from President Trump. We do not know yet the facts contained in the agents’ affidavit that goes with any warrant, but we certainly know enough to say this: These leftists’ accusation is laughable. The more likely scenario is Omar and many others will receive a Christmas present in the form of federal indictments. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION The Fourth Amendment bars judges from issuing a warrant without probable cause. U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh of the District of Columbia, the DC duty judge when the Omar raid occurred, reportedly signed the warrant for Omar’s home. That means Judge Sharbaugh found probable cause evidence of at least one federal crime is inside Omar’s home. Supreme Court precedents like United States v. Leon (1984) require that an issuing judge must be neutral and detached. If anything, Judge Sharbaugh's record suggests a judge predisposed to rule against the Trump Justice Department, not for it. articles.title: Ukraine defies Trump and launches one of its biggest drone attacks on Russia this year
articles.summary: Ukraine launched one of its biggest drone attacks this year on Russia overnight on Saturday, hitting a key oil terminal in defiance of US President Donald Trump’s demand it stop hitting Russian energy infrastructure.
articles.body: Ukraine launched one of its biggest drone attacks this year on Russia overnight on Saturday, hitting a key oil terminal in defiance of US President Donald Trump’s demand it stop hitting Russian energy infrastructure. There have been growing tensions between Ukraine and the US in recent days, prompting fears in Kyiv it could lose essential support as it approaches another winter under relentless Russian attack. But Ukraine is keeping up long-range strikes into Russia. Russia’s defense ministry said it shot down 1,015 Ukrainian drones overnight into Sunday over various parts of the country. One target was the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, according to Russian authorities. The terminal can handle up to 12.5 million tons per year. Ukraine’s Fire Point company, which makes the drones used in the attack, said there was a fire on the terminal’s grounds following the strike. A logistics centers in St. Petersburg was also attacked, according to Ozon, a Russian distribution company. One person was killed and five wounded by the attacks, with residential homes damaged as well, according to local authorities. Ukraine’s strikes come amid President Volodymyr Zelensky’s deteriorating relationship with Trump, who last week called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace.” A week ago Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure, as the White House tries to relieve pressure on oil and diesel prices ahead of crucial midterm elections. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow acknowledged such an agreement. Ukraine briefly halted such attacks, but has since resumed them — while Russia never stopped pounding Ukraine’s energy plants and cities. Eleven people were killed and nearly 50 injured across Ukraine in Russian missile and drone attacks in the 24 hours to Sunday morning, according to Ukrainian authorities, including what they called a massive attack on energy facilities in the Odesa region. “Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ​ago, Russia has ​deliberately ‌attacked ​Ukraine’s energy and oil and gas sectors ⁠76 times,” Zelensky ​wrote on X Sunday. “America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” Zelensky said. “On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting.” Trump has waived sanctions on imports of Russian diesel and on Friday invoked a waiver exempting Russia from sweeping economic penalties mandated by the US Congress, sparking criticism even from Republicans. Zelensky has also said that the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink system to guide its short-range and battlefield drones remains curtailed. “The maximum speed today is 161 kilometers per hour. After that, based on what I’ve seen and heard in the reports, Starlink shuts down, and we lose the drone,” he said Saturday. Zelensky said the restrictions have an impact on Ukraine’s defenses as well. “Unfortunately, we can’t currently use Starlink or Starshield any more in our country to shoot down jet-powered shaheds,” referring to the drone that have wrought so much damage in Ukraine. Starshield is a more advanced system designed for government and national-security needs. “The restrictions are in effect on Ukrainian territory, but they do not apply within the European Union. In other words, this is a planned operation… to restrict us, cut us off and prevent us from defending ourselves and protecting our people,” the Ukrainian president said Saturday. The Trump administration denies restricting the service. Last week Kyiv also said it was now facing Russian ballistic missile attacks without any alerts from allies. US satellite networks have been critical in providing the Ukrainian military with warnings of incoming missiles.

articles.title: Cornish gleaning group hits million milestone for food banks
articles.summary: Gleaning Cornwall warns that more funding is needed as costs rise sharply.
articles.body:
A gleaning group has saved £1m worth of fruit and vegetables that would have been left in field and donated them to food banks.

Gleaning Cornwall relies on volunteers to collect unwanted produce from harvested fields, delivering it to 160 food banks, community larders and kitchens across the South West.

Despite reaching the seven-figure milestone, the group has warned more funding is needed in order to keep up with demand.

Reliance on food banks is increasing and since 2015 the number of known settings providing food aid in Cornwall has risen from 20 to 180, according to Cornwall Council.

Gleaning Cornwall started in 2020 and said it had repurposed more than 460 tonnes of produce since then.

But the charity's founder, Holly Whitelaw, warned it was now threatened by economic constraints.

"There is less money around and we need to do more with it," she said. "Our infrastructure urgently needs funding if we are to keep going."

The charity said it fed 11,000 people every week with the stipulation that all its produce must be completely free to recipients.

However, the organisation said the cost of transport, storage and coordination was rising sharply.

It comes at a time when food bank usage is higher than ever with statistics from Cornwall's Trussell Trust showing its food banks distributed more than 35,500 emergency food parcels between April 2024 and March 2025.

A study by Cornwall Council found that 30% of children in the county are living in food poverty.

Whitelaw encouraged people to play their part by reducing the amount of food they wasted at home.

She said: "If we waste food, we waste the substantial energy that went into producing it.

"Utilising what we already have saves money and helps the environment."
